Tectonophystcs, 122: 165-185. Paleomagnetic investigations have been carried out on samples from the plutonic series of the Champ du Feu Massif and the Devonian-Ordovician host rocks. In order to date the different phases of magnetization, a series of samples has been selected for K-Ar analysis on micas, amphiboles and feldspars. The diorites, granodiorites, diabases and hornfelses are characterized by high susceptibilities of up to lo- ’ (Sl). Thermal demagnetization reveals several groups of directions of characteristic magnetiza- tion. The A direction: D = 202”, I = -23” (49’N, 153OE) is consistent with the Permian virtual geomagnetic pole for Europe. The B, direction: D = 59”. I = -22”(11°N, 128.5”E) was obtained from the effusive parts of the Kagenfels granite dated at 284 Ma. Diorites, microdiorites and volcanics, emplaced a short time after the intrusion of the Natzwiller granite, dated at 344 and 351 Ma, display three groups of directions; the C, direction: D = 328’, I = -15O (27”N, 223S”E), the Cz: D = 323O, i = -38” (13% 222-E) and the C,: D = 272”. PALEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING AND LABORATORY TECHNIQUES Oriented samples were drilled in situ or collected as handsamples. Whenever possible, they were oriented both with a solar and a magnetic compass. The handsamples were cored in the laboratory and the cores subsequently cut into standard specimens 2.5 cm long. Remanent magnetization measurements were performed on a computerized Digico magnetometer, with noise level reduced to 3 . lo-’ Am-‘. Susceptibilities were determined with a Digico susceptibility bridge. The alternating field and thermal demagnetizations were done with laboratory-made apparatus. NATURAL REMANENT MAGNETIZATIONS AND SUSCEPTIBILITIES High magnetic anomalies of up to 300 nT at 1200 m above sea level overlie the northern Vosges. They belong to a band of anomalies which extends from the Paris Basin to the Thuringerwald (Edel. 1982). Their origin is attributed to the magnetic properties of granodiorites, diorites and rocks of contact metamorphism (Lauer and Taktak, 1971; Edel and Lauer, 1974; Lauer, 1975; Gancarski, 1977). The results presented here were obtained from plutonic and volcano-sedimentary units from the northern Vosges. The objectives of the study were first to improve our knowledge of the magnetic properties of the plutons, second to assess the impact. in terms of rock magnetism, of their intrusion on the surrounding host rocks and third to check whether the basement on both sides of the Lalaye-Lubine fault, which delimits the northern Vosges from the middle and southern, underwent simifar motions in Carboniferous times. K-Ar dating of plutonics on extracted minerals was carried out in order to assign ages to the successive magnetizations. GEOLOGICAL SETTING OF THE NORTHERN VOSGES The Vosges Massif is divided structuratly into two parts by an important fault trending E-W, called the “Lalaye-Lubine dislocation”. The domain, situated to the north, belongs to the Saxothuringian zone (Kossmat, 1927) whereas the southern one is part of the Moldanubian zone. This zone of dislocation successively acted as a south-dipping thrust fault and then as a dextral strike-slip fault with an offset of about 100 km (Edel, 1982). Since the Permian Nideck-Donon ignimbrites indicate a similar direction (Roche et al., 1962) the emplacement of magnetizations can be considered to be late. The A-direction belongs to the Kiaman reversed interval with a corresponding VGP which is consistent with European poles, i.e. the latest Carboniferous and Permian poles (Fig. 5). It has to be noted that this VGP is unique in the northern Vosges. The B,-direction is exhibited as a primary magnetization in the Kagenfels rhyolite and as overprinting in the neighbouring series, granodiorites and schists. A K-ear determination on biotite from the Kagenfels granite indicates an age of 284 Ma which corresponds to the Carboniferous-Permian boundary. Closely similar direc- tions exist in the northern and northeastern Massif Central (Edel et al.. 1981 b: Edel, 1984) where they have been observed in Carboniferous volcanics, plutons and amphibolites (Fig. 6). In the latter formation, the mean direction: D = 247”. I = 3.5” (VGP: 14”N. 1lO”E) represents an overprinting related to leucogranite intrusion dated at 312 Ma (Edel, 1984). Further west

is observed with mean direction D = 238”, I= - 8” (VGP: 24”N, 112”E) of which the declination can be compared with the reversed B,. This latter overprint occurred after the early Westphalian. Wandering of the paleomagnetic directions from B to A cannot be simply explained by tilting of the Champ du Feu massif to the southeast, since the dip would exceed 70”. Thus we are compelled to assume a StephanianAutunian clockwise rotation of the northern Vosges relative to the “stable Europe”. If the B,-direction is considered, the angle of rotation is about 30”. To the northeast of the Variscan chain, sedimentary layers from the IIarz mountains indicate a 20”.-30°- counterclockwise rotation, probably of Carboniferous age (Bachtadse et al.. 1983). The results presented here were obtained from plutonic and volcano-sedimentary units from the northern Vosges. The objectives of the study were first to improve our knowledge of the magnetic properties of the plutons, second to assess the impact. in terms of rock magnetism, of their intrusion on the surrounding host rocks and third to check whether the basement on both sides of the Lalaye-Lubine fault, which delimits the northern Vosges from the middle and southern, underwent simifar motions in Carboniferous times. The results presented here were obtained from plutonic and volcano-sedimentary units from the northern Vosges. The objectives of the study were first to improve our knowledge of the magnetic properties of the plutons, second to assess the impact. in terms of rock magnetism, of their intrusion on the surrounding host rocks and third to check whether the basement on both sides of the Lalaye-Lubine fault, which delimits the northern Vosges from the middle and southern, underwent simifar motions in Carboniferous times. K-Ar dating of plutonics on extracted minerals was carried out in order to assign ages to the successive magnetizations. GEOLOGICAL SETTING OF THE NORTHERN VOSGES The Vosges Massif is divided structuratly into two parts by an important fault trending E-W, called the “Lalaye-Lubine dislocation”. The domain, situated to the north, belongs to the Saxothuringian zone (Kossmat, 1927) whereas the southern one is part of the Moldanubian zone. This zone of dislocation successively acted as a south-dipping thrust fault and then as a dextral strike-slip fault with an offset of about 100 km (Edel, 1982). 6. Paleomagnetism of Lower Carboniferous (Tournaisian to Namurian) volcanic rocks of New Brunswick, Canada, and its tectonic implications. Tecfonophysics, 122: 357-379. Following Kent and Opdyke’s (1978) hypothesis, the possibility that a sinistral motion north of the Maine coastal volcanic belt has brought the New England-Canadian Maritimes region to its present position with respect to cratonic North America during the Carboniferous time was tested by a paleomagnetic study of gently dipping Lower Carboniferous volcanic rocks of New Brunswick. After removal of a low unblocking (T,,) and low coercivity component variably present in the samples, a single coherent mean remanence direction was isolated: D = 161”. I = + ll”, K = 78 and q5 = 5.5” for N = 10 sites (42 samples), characterized by a high T UR (450’-66O’C) linear vector trajectory present in each sample. The corresponding paleomagnetic pole falls at 136”E. 36ON (d, = 5.6”, d, = 2.8”). This pole is not significantly different from Early Carboniferous poles from the stable North American (NA) craton. If any left-lateral relative motion in the Carboniferous took place, it is not located in the Maritimes New England region but further north, closer to the craton, in the northern New Brunswick-southeastern Quebec region.

INTRODUCTION The volcanic flows sampled for paleomagnetic purposes are located in two tectonic zones (Fig. 1): (1) on the New Brunswick Platform which forms a flat-lying Carboniferous cover unconformably overlying Silurian sedimentary rocks of the Frederiction Trough but overlapping the Cambro-Ordovician Miramichi Massif in the northeast; (2) within two Carboniferous outliers lying unconformably over Upper Silurian and Lower Devonian volcanic and sedimentary rocks on the south- east margin of the Late Ordovician to Early Devonian Matapedia Basin (Fyffe et al., 1981). The Miramichi Massif lies within the Gander Zone of Williams (1978) which in New Brunswick is separated f

The northeastern Matapedia Basin contains a fault block of Ordovician ophiolitic rocks (Rast and Stringer, 1980) included within the Dunnage Zone (Williams, 1978). Specimens were subjected to alternating field and thermal demagnetization. Two mean magnetization directions, which are approximately antipodal, were found. Three Upper Triassic-Lower Jurassic formations in southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico have been investigated paleomagnetically as a means of testing for displacement along the proposed Mojave-Sonora megashear. Liming Formation of west-central Nevada and Sil Nakya Forma- tion of southern Arizona lie north of the megashear whereas, in northwestern Sonora, Antimonio Formation lies south of the megashear. Previously published results from the Nazas Formation of presumed Lower Jurassic age from north-central Mexico were incorporated into the interpretations. These four units compose two sets of correlative formations

The displacement needed to bring all of these poles into coincidence is a pure rotation of about 8” counterclockwise about the sampling area. Two probable Cretaceous poles were obtained from the Sand Wells Formation of southern Arizona and from unnamed volcanics in northwest Sonora. These poles are essentially identical and suggest that displacement along the megashear had ceased by the Cretaceous. Data from the Early Jurassic Mulberry Wash and Pitoikam formations in southern Arizona appear to have been remagnetized in a later Cretaceous event and were not used in this study. nding suites of diabase dikes which crosscut one another have been identified in the North Carolina Piedmont from the interpretation of aeromagnetic data and field relationships (e.g., Popenoe and Zietz, 1977; Burt et al., 1978). The crosscutting relationships and area1 distribution of the dikes suggest that they were emplaced during two different stress regimes representing different ages or phases of the Early Mesozoic rifting of the North American margin. A paleomagnetic study was conducted on the two crosscutting dike suites of the North Carolina Piedmont in order to establish whether the time differential in the emplacement of the dike suites was significant or not and to confirm relative ages. Results from 11 NW trending diabase dike sites yield a VGP of 52.8’ N, 60.2” E. The VGP for 15 N-S trending diabase dike sites is located at 71.5 ON, 53.5’ E. The Fisherian statistics of the pole position for both suites are significantly different from one another. This therefore suggests a relative age differential for the emplacement of diabase dikes with the NW suite interpreted as being relatively older than the N-S suite of dikes. lting of the Piedmont province of this region. The systematic regional distribution of diabase dikes in eastern North America was first pointed out by King (1961, 1971). Since then the dikes have been related to the tensional tectonic events associated with the breakup of Pangea in the Early Mesosoic (De Boer, 1967; May, 1971; Swanson, 1982). Throughout eastern North America, the Meso- zoic diabase has been the subject of numerous geochemical, paleomagnetic and geochronological studies. Most work on the paleomagnetism of diabase dikes, flows, and sills has been done in the northern Appalachians {e.g., Irving and Banks, 1961; Opdyke, 1961; Larochelle and Wanless, 1966; De Boer, 1967,1968; Larochelle, 1967,1971; Carmichael and Palmer, 1968; Beck, 1972; Smith and Noltimier, 1979; Hodych and Hayatsu, 1980; Sequin et al., 1981). Only a few studies on diabase dikes (De Boer, 1968; Watts, 1975: Bell et al., 1980; Dooley and Smith, 1982) and subsurface flows (Phillips, 1983) have been carried out in the southern Appalachians. nding suites of diabase dikes which crosscut one another have been identified in the North Carolina Piedmont from the interpretation of aeromagnetic data and field relationships (e.g., Popenoe and Zietz, 1977; Burt et al., 1978). The crosscutting relationships and area1 distribution of the dikes suggest that they were emplaced during two different stress regimes representing different ages or phases of the Early Mesozoic rifting of the North American margin. A paleomagnetic study was conducted on the two crosscutting dike suites of the North Carolina Piedmont in order to establish whether the time differential in the emplacement of the dike suites was significant or not and to confirm relative ages. Results from 11 NW trending diabase dike sites yield a VGP of 52.8’ N, 60.2” E. The VGP for 15 N-S trending diabase dike sites is located at 71.5 ON, 53.5’ E. The Fisherian statistics of the pole position for both suites are significantly different from one another. This therefore suggests a relative age differential for the emplacement of diabase dikes with the NW suite interpreted as being relatively older than the N-S suite of dikes. This therefore suggests a relative age differential for the emplacement of diabase dikes with the NW suite interpreted as being relatively older than the N-S suite of dikes. The pole positions of both suites plot off the APW path for North America. To bring these aberrant poles into near coincidence with the APW path for North America would require the tilting of the Piedmont westwards approximately 15 ‘. However, there is no geological evidence of a measurable amount of a probably complex post Jurassic tilting of the Piedmont province of this region. The systematic regional distribution of diabase dikes in eastern North America was first pointed out by King (1961, 1971). Since then the dikes have been related to the tensional tectonic events associated with the breakup of Pangea in the Early Mesosoic (De Boer, 1967; May, 1971; Swanson, 1982). It was assumed that data observed might be explained by diagenetic compaction of sediments. Such a hypothesis has already been proposed (e.g., Laj et al., 1982), although without numerical evaluation. If correct, this hypothesis leads to some important conclusions: (1) As compaction of sediments takes place mainly at early stages of diagenesis, such a corre- lation implies that magnetization must be either contemporaneous with sedimentation in case of DRM or quasicontemporaneous with it in case of post-depositional DRM and early diagenetic CRM. Thus, the strong correlation between in- clination and clay content confirms the primary origin of stable magnetization in the Upper Creta- ceous-Paleocene rocks and, in general, such an approach may be used for component dating. (2) Only the largest values of inclination should be used for paleolatitude estimation. In this paper, these are the data from limestones at sites 6, 9, 10 and 11. The overall mean for all types of rocks studied will lead to errors. The steepest inclina- tions also may be shallow, but such a selection will result in minimal errors. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. It is connected with the distension which occurred in the Pyreneo-Cantabrian region during the upper Jurassic-lower Cretaceous. The main remagnetization phase which occurred after the folding is dated from the lower Tertiary, and can be related to the compression induced on the northern boundary of Iberia from upper Cretaceous onwards. In some cases this phase led to a complete replacement of the primary magnetization. Previously published data, which were at the time interpreted as being European-like in direction, are attributed to this phase. Hence, our results do not support the hypothesis of a micro-plate called “le Danois block”, which was suggested in order to explain these results. GeologIcal setting and description of the sam- pling localities 2.1. Cantabric chain (Fig. I) The redbeds are exposed on the eastern border of the Paleozoic Asturian massif. They are found discordantly overlying either shales of unknown age or Carboniferous limestone. Saiz de Omenaca (1977) divides the continental deposits into two or three sedimentary cycles depending on locality. In the sampled area, sedimentation apparently began later than in the western basins (Sierras de Pena Sagra, Pena Labra, Hijar) and comprised only two cycles, reaching a thickness of 100 and 260 m respectively. In the kinematic model proposed by Vandenberg, this prominent feature might represent the southern boundary of the “Le Danois block”. The whole area was cer- tainly involved in the tectonic events which de- formed the Spanish margin during the Eocene and Oligocene. This idea was challenged some years ago by the paleomagnetic data ob- tained by Vandenberg (1979) in a small Mesozoic basin located in the Asturias. Surprisingly, the Permo-Triassic redbeds yielded directions ap- parently very similar to Permo-Triassic data from stable Europe. He attempted to explain this unex- pected result by postulating the existence of a micro-plate, called “Le Danois block”, which would have behaved independently during the major movement of the Iberian plate coeval with the opening of the Bay of Biscay. The reasons supporting the assigned Permo-Triassic age to the magnetic components were: (1) Since the NRM behaved as a single compo- 0040-1951/87/$03.50 0 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. 180 nent, there was no evidence for any remagnetiza- tion. (2) Both polarities, although not exactly anti- parallel, were found. (3) The dip correction of the monoclinal struc- ture resulted in shallow inclinations consistent with the assumed Permo-Triassic age of magnetization. As there was little geological evidence support- ing Vandenberg’s hypothesis, his results called for further investigation. Our aim was mainly (1) to verify or refute Vandenberg’s paleomagnetic inter- pretation using more data, and (2) to delimit the “le Danois block” more closely. Fossil plants from our study area indicate a Siegenian age for the sediments (Thomas, 1978). Sampling and laboratory treatment For our study we sampled a well-exposed southeasterly plunging fold in a roadside quarry near Milford Haven, South Wales (open star in Fig. 1). A set of thin dikes from central New Mexico, dated at 469& 7 Ma (Rb-Sr; Loring and Armstrong, 1980), have yielded a virtual geomagnetic pole which lies on the Late Paleozoic segment of the North American apparent polar wander path. The remanence of the dikes appears to be a product of Late Paleozoic hydrothermal alteration. Paradoxically, however, the magnetization of the host rocks is most simply explained in terms of a positive contact test. Samples collected between 0.2 and 0.5 dike-widths from the contact contain a component of remanence parallel to the magnetization in the dikes, with unblocking temperatures which decrease with distance from the dikes. Host rocks from a distance of more than 1 dike-width show no evidence of the characteristic dike magnetization. There are two possible resolutions of this paradox: (1) the magnetization of the host rocks is secondary, despite the apparent positive contact test, and is a product of hydrothe~al fluid migration through the dikes or along the contact zones; or (2) the magnetization of the dikes is primary, but not representative of the Ordovician paleofield for North America. Possible reasons for inaccurate representation include: (a) incomplete averaging of secular variation; (b) tectonic rota

al uplift (Fig. l), and have been described by Loring and Armstrong (1980). Three thin trachytic dikes in the Pedernal Hills and a stock at Lobo Hill consist of a distinctive brick-red syenite and in- trude lower greenschist facies quartz-sericite and quartz-chlorite schists of the Precambrian Tor- rance Metamorphic Group (Muehlberger et al., 1966; Foster et al., 1972; Grambling, 1986). The dike rocks are unfoliated and unmetamorphosed, but the host rocks exhibit a well-developed folia- tion, generally parallel to the dikes. Both the intrusives and the adjacent host rocks show signs of alteration and secondary minerali- zation. Petrographically the syenite consists of ap- proximately 60-70% alkali feldspar, partially re- placed by very fine clay minerals; 10% quartz; and 2% opaque minerals, predominantly hematite with minor magnetite (Loring and Armstrong, 1980). The iron oxides occur both as finely disseminated grains and in a pattern resembling an amphibole crystal habit, suggesting an origin by replacement of hornblende (Loring and Armstrong, 1980). Other secondary minerals include sericite, calcite, and siderite. Following measurement of the natural rema- nent ma~etization (NRM) of the dikes and host rocks, all samples were subjected to stepwise de- magnetization by alternating-field (AF) or thermal methods. Collinear and coplanar segments of the demagnetization trajectories were isolated by visu- al inspection of orthogonal vector projections (Zijderveld, 1967) and stereographic projections. Directions were determined by principal compo- nent analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) and means were computed using the method of Bailey and Halls (1984). Several rock magnetic experiments were per- formed in order to characterize the remanence carriers. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) was imparted in a stepwise manner to a number of samples of the dike and host rocks, using an electromagnet, up to a peak field of 1.4 T. Thermomagnetic analysis of magnetic separates from several dike and host samples was performed with a horizontal Curie balance. Modified Lowrie-Fuller tests (Johnson et al., 1975) were performed in order to elucidate the domain state of magnetites in the host rock. Paleomagnetic measurements on as- phaltic samples from two formations in southern Oklahoma have been performed. A bioclastic unit from the Boggy Formation, known as the Buckhorn asphalt, exhibited a stable, characteristic remanent moment (RM) after A.F. demagnetization between 5-20 mT. We infer from our data that very fine, pos- sibly authigenic magnetite, like that shown to have a genetic relationship with the migration through rocks of hydrocarbons [Elmore et a1.,1987], is the primary RM carrier in these samples. The tilt cor- rected paleopole for the Buckhorn asphalt (121.9 E; 43.5 N; p= 1.3; m = 2.3) falls on the Early Permian Apparent Polar Wander Path for North America of Irving and Irving [1982], using a 30 Ma window (270-280 Ma). Introduction Previous paleomagnetic measurements on rocks containing hydrocarbons, such as the Athabasca Oil Sands in Alberta, Canada [Ellwood and Pem- berton, 1984] and some Utah oil shales [Richardson and Noltimier, 1980], have demonstrated that these rocks may carry a stable remanent moment (RM). Recent work by Elmore et al., [1987] has shown that very fine grained (<3 m), and abundant authigenic magnetite was produced during hydrocarbon migr- ation through Permian limestones in southern Ok- lahoma. These magnetite grains, associated with hydrocarbons are expected to carry a stable RM. At The University of Texas at Arlington (UTA), we have been examining the magnetic properties of rocks from the Arbuckle Mountain region, for the purposes of joint magnetostratigraphic-biostrati- graphic studies. Our results have been disappoint- ing, primarily because these rocks appear to have been remagnetized. This remagnetization may be due to a number of factors, including the oxidation of unstable minerals, iron oxides, sulfides and car- bonates, leading to the development of stable but secondary RM carriers. From a stratigraphic point of view, this region is characterized by a thick Mesozoic carbonate platform, consisting of over 6000 meters of reef, back reef and dolomitic limestones, which conformably overlie an only gently deformed Paleozoic basement. A series of well stratified (150 m thick) limestones with rich microfauna, known as 'Calcari di Castro' were deposited during the Eocene and Oligocene. Although this formation is mostly of a rather coarse material, very fine grained levels can be found interbedded with the coral-algal strata. During the Miocene large amounts of calcarenites, limestones and yellow sands, the 'Pietra Leccese' formation, was also deposited over most of the region. Finally during the Pliocene and the Early Pleistocene coarse grained calcarenites and organogenic sands, known as 'Calcareniti del Salento' were deposited during marine transgressive events. From a tectonic point of view, the main feature of the Salento is the Cretaceous carbonatic-dolomitic ridge which coincides, to a lust approximation, with old Mesozoic reef zones. The natural remanent magnetizations in some upper Cambrian and middle Ordovician limestones from the Taconics of Vermont (~44øN 287øE) are multicomponent and can be attributed to early Paleozoic, late Paleozoic and Cretaceous-early Tertiary remagnetizations. A northwesterly and up magnetization found at 2 sampling localities, characterized by maximum unblocking temperatures of about 350øC, has directions prior to tilt correction corresponding to Ordovician reference poles for North America and is likely to represent a Taconic remagnetization. A shallow, southerly magnetization found at a third locality, with unblocking temperatures that range to about 500øC, has directions corresponding to a Permian (Kiaman and Alleghenian) remagnetization. Common to all 3 sampling localities is a low (up to 300øC) unblocking temperature overprint similar in direction to Cretaceous to Paleocene reference poles. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Orwell-1 samples (14 oriented drill-cores from 2 sites) were taken from an old quarry off Cider Mill Road, near Middlebury. section_candidates.excerpt: Appalachian carbonates affected by the Ordovician Taconic Orogeny. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Geology and Sampling The structure of the study area in west-central Vermont is a product of the Taconic Orogeny during the Ordovician and is summarized by Stanley and Ratcliffe [1985]. Horizontal compression related to eastward subduction and a collision with an island arc folded the carbonate platform into the Middlebury Synclinorium. Deep-sea sediments from the continental slope and rise were incorporated into the accretionary prism and eventually were obducted onto the folded carbonate platform producing the allochthonous Taconic thrust slices. Orwell-1 samples (14 oriented drill-cores from 2 sites) were taken from an old quarry off Cider Mill Road, near Middlebury. Orwell-2 samples (21 oriented drill cores from 3 sites) were taken from a quarry in Orwell. Each sampling group represents 5 to 10 m of section in gently dipping (less than 20 ø ) beds. The third group of samples was taken from the Hatch Hill Formation in the Giddingsbrook Slice of the Taconic Allochthon, near Fair Haven. This section of the Hatch Hill Formation consists of black to grey argillite beds with interbeds of dolostone, sandstone, chert breccia, and limestone. Baldwin [ 1983] has suggested a late Cambrian age for these rocks using lithostratigraphic correlations with the autochthonous shelf sequence. Hatch Hill samples (56 oriented drill-cores from 8 sites) were taken in steeply dipping to overturned beds exposed along the Poultney River. But the in-field directions display a suggestive distribution: the declinations are scattered whereas the inclinations are well-grouped between 40 o and 50 O. Taking into account the tectonic implication of the primary directions, we suggest that the distribution of directions observed results from two successive tectonic phases: (1) folding with subhorizontal axes and (2) clockwise rotations around the vertical axes. The paleomagnetic study of Permo-Triassic red bed outcrops located in several basement units and slices of the western Pyrenees is presented. Despite strong overprintings attributed to remagnetization processes connected with the early Tertiary compressional phase, we were able to identify the original magnetization in all sites. The directions yielded reveal the occurrence, in the whole area, of clockwise rotations, varying, with respect to the European reference direction, from nearly O” to 102O. The secondary directions are interpreted as more or less contemporary with the inferred rotations. The paleomagnetic data are discussed in the light of two kinematic models for the Iberian plate. The examination of the models involving a left-lateral displacement of Iberia during the mid-Cretaceous is most conclusive and leads us to suggest that, at that time, the boundary between Europe and Iberia was located south of the Cinco-Villas and Aldudes massifs. Paleomagnetism of Permo-Triassic red beds in the western Pyrenees: evidence for strong clockwise rotations of the Paleozoic units. Tectonophysics, 156: 75-88. The paleomagnetic study of Permo-Triassic red bed outcrops located in several basement units and slices of the western Pyrenees is presented. Despite strong overprintings attributed to remagnetization processes connected with the early Tertiary compressional phase, we were able to identify the original magnetization in all sites. The directions yielded reveal the occurrence, in the whole area, of clockwise rotations, varying, with respect to the European reference direction, from nearly O” to 102O. The secondary directions are interpreted as more or less contemporary with the inferred rotations. The paleomagnetic data are discussed in the light of two kinematic models for the Iberian plate. The examination of the models involving a left-lateral displacement of Iberia during the mid-Cretaceous is most conclusive and leads us to suggest that, at that time, the boundary between Europe and Iberia was located south of the Cinco-Villas and Aldudes massifs. The anomalous westerly magnetizations of the second highest flow remain unexplained, although they may represent direc- tions acquired during a transitional field. INTRODUCTION McWilliams and Kroner (1981) showed that the 1,2 to 0,5 Ga old palaeomagnetic poles for the Congo and Kalahari shields (a total of 41 poles) could be incorporated into a single apparent polar wander (APW) path. From this observation, they derived an ensialic model for the origin of the Damara Orogen that did not require large-scale opening and closing of ocean basins, characteristic of a Wilson-cycle process. As they clearly indicated, however, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Kalahari Shield lie on the 1,2 to 1 Ga portion of their APW path; whereas, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Congo Shield lie on the 0,9 to 0,6 Ga por

y a very few poles actually overlap from the two shields. Two of these poles were derived from a previously published palaeomagnetic study of the Gannakouriep dyke swarm (Piper, 1975a), which were referred to as the Klein Karas and the pre­ N ama dykes. The ages of these poles were purportedly-850 and -650 Ma respectively, which coincide with the peak of the tectonic evolution of the Damara Orogen. The apparent agreement of these poles with poles from the Congo Shield is obviously of paramount importance to plate tectonic models for the origin of the Damara Oro gen. For this reason, the authors undertook a detailed palaeomagnetic, petrographic, and 40Ar/39Ar study of two dykes belonging to the Gannakouriep dyke swarm with the goal of either verifying and improving upon the previously published results or refuting them. INTRODUCTION McWilliams and Kroner (1981) showed that the 1,2 to 0,5 Ga old palaeomagnetic poles for the Congo and Kalahari shields (a total of 41 poles) could be incorporated into a single apparent polar wander (APW) path. From this observation, they derived an ensialic model for the origin of the Damara Orogen that did not require large-scale opening and closing of ocean basins, characteristic of a Wilson-cycle process. As they clearly indicated, however, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Kalahari Shield lie on the 1,2 to 1 Ga portion of their APW path; whereas, most of the palaeomagnetic poles from the Congo Shield lie on the 0,9 to 0,6 Ga portion. In fact, only a very few poles actually overlap from the two shields. Two of these poles were derived from a previously published palaeomagnetic study of the Gannakouriep dyke swarm

GEOLOGIC SETTING Ohio Range The Ohio Range comprises a prominent 1000 m granitic escarpment separating the Polar Plateau to the south from the great ice sheet of Marie Byrd Land to the north (Fig. 1). Ordovician granitic basement rocks (Treves 1965) compose most of the steep escarpment, and are overlain by a mostly flat lying, 1200 m thick sequence of nonmetamorphosed sedimentary rocks of Devonian and Permian age (Long 1965; Bradshaw et al. 1984; McCartan et al. 1986). A prominent basaltic dolerite sill, correlated with the Ferrar Dolerite, intrudes the upper part of the sedimentary sequence (Treves 1965). The basement rocks of the Ohio Range are part of the Wisconsin Range batholith (Mirsky 1969), inferred to have been emplaced during the Late Cambrian-Ordovician Ross Orogeny (Gunn & Warren 1962). Abstract Two well-defined virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) for East Antarctica were obtained from the Middle Jurassic Ferrar Dolerite, sampled from a thick sill on Mt Schopf in the Ohio Range, and from a horizontal sheet intruding Paleozoic granitic rocks at Mt Cerberus in the Dry Valleys. The VGP from the sill at Mt Schopf lies at lat. 58°.0S, long. 129°.0W (dm=13°, dp=12°), and the VGP from Mt Cerberus lies at lat. 57°.8S, long. 135°.7W (dm=6°, dp=6°). Rocks from both localities have normal polarity magnetisations. These data, together with 15 other acceptable pole positions reported in the literature, define a Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic pole at 52°.7S, 139°.6W (u9s=4°A), which is not significantly different from previously reported mean Middle Jurassic paleomagnetic poles from East Antarctica. Paleomagnetic investigations in the Ohio Range of mafic inclusions in Ordovician granitic and sedimentary rocks of Devonian and Permian ages found that the rocks are magnetically unstable and are unreliable for determining a paleomagnetic pole. GEOLOGIC SETTING Ohio Range The Ohio Range comprises a prominent 1000 m granitic escarpment separating the Polar Plateau to the south from the great ice sheet of Marie Byrd Land to the north (Fig. 1). As there appears to be no relationship between this activity and the plate boundaries, a linear mantle source has been proposed (Adams 1981; Wellman 1983). Four of these centres in South Island were selected for paleomagnetic study: the Dunedin volcano, the Lyttelton volcano, the Akaroa volcano, and the Diamond Harbour Group (Fig. I). These all lie in regions which are considered not to have been affected by later tectonic activity (Walcott 1984). From the mean K-Ar dates calculated for the section (Evans 1970) the mean age for the bottom of the section (this study) is 9.0 ±0.2 Ma and for the top is 8.6 ± 0.2 Ma. This makes correlation of the top normal period with subchron 4Ar-2 (8.80 - 8.87 Ma) the most likely (Fig. 10). This was the correla­ tion favoured by Evans (1970). The lower N-R tran­ sition will correlate with the top of chron 5 and the reversed interval found by Evans (1970) at about 70 m above sea level will correspond to subchron 5-1. DIAMOND HARBOUR GROUP The last stages of volcanism on Banks Peninsula were fairly localised eruptions (SewellI988), often infilling valleys eroded in the earlier Lyttelton flows. The activity was mainly centred around Quail Island and the Diamond Harbour area. Liggett & Gregg (1965) divided these late alkali basalts into three formations which together comprised their Diamond Harbour Group. The Church Formation usually has well-developed columnar jointing in its flows, whereas the Kaioruru Formation appears coarse grained, often forming pahoehoe flows, and the Stoddart Formation forms aa flows with well-developed flow breccias. The three formations are on the shore at Church Bay, with angular unconformities

le position. Thus a tectonic origin for the far and near sidedness of the two younger centres may be discounted. STORETVEDT Institute of Geophysics, University of Bergen, 5000 Bergen, Norway SYNOPSIS Palaeomagnetic results from the Sarclet Sandstone Formation, stratig- raphically positioned near the base of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) sequence of Caithness, suggest the presence of two different axes of magnetization, with Dec. 211, Inc. 33 and Dec. 191, Inc. 6 respectively. Complex multiphase magnetiza­ tions have been uncovered in most of these cases, and for various Caithness rocks a substantial fraction of the original Devonian remanence appears to have been erased during Permo-Mesozoic remagnetization. On the whole, the total palaeomagnetic record has gradually become better understood and as a conse­ quence a number of potential applications of the results to local geological problems can now be envisaged. inal titano-magnetite (TM) grains of the Devonian tuff layer of Hoy have undergone a complete oxidation in that all TM particles now tend to consist of haematite and rutile. The more severe oxidation state of the tuff, as compared to that of the lavas, is in part attributed to its fairly porous character. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. The present investigation is believed to have been quite successful in this respect, and the results appear to have interesting implications for tectonic and age problems. Complex multiphase magnetiza­ tions have been uncovered in most of these cases, and for various Caithness rocks a substantial fraction of the original Devonian remanence appears to have been erased during Permo-Mesozoic remagnetization. On the whole, the total palaeomagnetic record has gradually become better understood and as a conse­ quence a number of potential applications of the results to local geological problems can now be envisaged. inal titano-magnetite (TM) grains of the Devonian tuff layer of Hoy have undergone a complete oxidation in that all TM particles now tend to consist of haematite and rutile. The more severe oxidation state of the tuff, as compared to that of the lavas, is in part attributed to its fairly porous character. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. GENERAL GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING At the base of the Hoy Sandstone of Upper Old Red Sandstone age (Sedgwick and Murchison 1828; Wilson et al. 1935; Halliday et al. 1977) a volcanic horizon is exposed at a few localities notably in the northern part of the island (Fig. 1). The volcanicity was of explosive character and an ashy deposit with thicknesses ranging upward to c. 15 m was laid down prior to lava outpouring. In the various lava outcrops only one flow is recognized at any one locality, and the petrography is always that of an olivine basalt with phenocrysts of olivine, pyroxene and feldspar (Wilson et al. 1935). Faults occur between the separate igneous exposures, and from field evidence it is impossible to be certain of the precise stratigraphical relation between the outcrops. In northern Hoy the volcanics rest on Middle Old Red Sandstone strata and between these sediments and the overlying Hoy Sandstone there is a fairly marked tectonic unconformity. Thus, given rocks like the Orkney volcanics, one must anticipate a lengthy magnetization record of unknown duration. The palaeomagnetic structure of such rocks would normally be a complex one (as was also demonstrated in the earlier study), but provided individual palaeomagnetic components can be successfully extracted, important information on the geological history of the region might be deduced. In view of the progress in palaeomagnetic instrumentation and techniques over the past 15 years, it was decided to re-assess the palaeomagnetism of the Hoy volcanics with the hope of achieving more information than that obtained in the original study. The present investigation is believed to have been quite successful in this respect, and the results appear to have interesting implications for tectonic and age problems. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. DISCUSSION The mean directions for the nine deposits are shown in Fig. 3. All are normally magnetised except Mogo Hill, Barrenjoey and Peat's Ridge, which are reversely magnetised. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. Recent work by Schmidt (1976) demon- strates that the pole positions from this earlier palaeomagnetic work result from directions in which secondary components have not been entirely elimi- nated, and his mean Jurassic pole position (MJP), from rocks subjected to more severe laboratory treatment, is also shown in Fig. 4. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. They are consist- ent with a hypothesis that the intrusions into the Sydney Basin came in several pulses (Manwaring, 1963) that can be differentiated, in some cases, by differences in their magnetisation directions and the pole positions calculated from them. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. On the other hand, Hamilton et al (1970) suggest that, on the evidence of coal reflectance figures from fragments found in these breccias, the temper- ature of formation must have been less than 100°C. Two possible solutions to this inconsistency may be considered. Firstly, the temperature within the breccias may have varied from less than 100° to more than 400°C at the time of consolidation. Secondly, chemical alterations in the low temperature ranges may have caused the formation of magnetic minerals, most probably iron oxides that acquired a chemical remanence which itself had higher blocking temperatures. DISCUSSION The mean directions for the nine deposits are shown in Fig. 3. All are normally magnetised except Mogo Hill, Barrenjoey and Peat's Ridge, which are reversely magnetised. It is not possible to tell how much of secular variation has been averaged by the time spread of the samples, as the rate at which the acquisition of the magnetisation spread through the deposits is not known. Hence an unknown, but probably small, secular variation error is likely to be present in all the results. Bearing this in mind, Figure 3. Pole positions for other intrusions into the Sydney Basin, of which the directions had been previously determined, (Boesen et al., 1961; Manwaring, 1963) are also shown in Fig. 4. PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS 35 Gilbraltar, Prospect and Gingenbullen have been radiogenically dated (Evernden and Richards, 1962) and appear to have been intruded during the Jurassic. Recent work by Schmidt (1976) demon- strates that the pole positions from this earlier palaeomagnetic work result from directions in which secondary components have not been entirely elimi- nated, and his mean Jurassic pole position (MJP), from rocks subjected to more severe laboratory treatment, is also shown in Fig. 4. The results of this preliminary study show that there are significant differences in remanent magnetisation directions between different in- trusions into the Sydney Basin. They are consist- ent with a hypothesis that the intrusions into the Sydney Basin came in several pulses (Manwaring, 1963) that can be differentiated, in some cases, by differences in their magnetisation directions and the pole positions calculated from them.
